summary:
We developed AstroVitals, a prototype web application that helps astronauts understand and track their physical and psychological well-being throughout a space mission. It combines an interactive 3D body with clickable organ-system status, vital readings, daily wellness assessments, and a medical-officer dashboard showing crew health trends over time.

Our recovery-readiness model was trained using PMData’s sleep and activity data. Daily check-ins complement those readings by capturing symptoms, mood, stress, and isolation, with wellness summaries and optional AI-assisted guidance. A built-in Mission Guide explains the interface to first-time users.

AstroVitals addresses the challenge by bringing health indicators, self-assessment, and understandable visual feedback into one experience. NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework informed our physical and mental health focus. This matters because long-duration missions place greater responsibility on astronauts to recognize changes in their health and seek support.

The current demo uses simulated telemetry. Real wearable integration, privacy enforcement, and spaceflight validation are planned next steps. AstroVitals supports awareness and medical review—not diagnosis.
details:
We developed AstroVitals, a prototype web application for the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge. It brings physiological readings, recovery estimates, and physical and psychological check-ins into one experience for astronauts and medical officers.

Astronauts can explore an interactive 3D human body and select an organ system to view its status and supporting readings. The home dashboard and organ view share simulated monitoring data, including heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, and respiratory rate. A built-in Mission Guide introduces first-time users to the application’s main features.

In AI Analysis, users enter sleep and activity information. Our tree-based readiness model, trained using PMData’s sleep and activity data, processes these inputs to estimate recovery and classify readiness as Recover, Normal, or Hard. These categories support awareness; they are not medical clearance for exercise. PMData is an Earth-based dataset, not NASA astronaut data.

Daily assessments capture information that readings alone cannot provide, including symptoms, energy, sleep quality, mood, stress, isolation, and motivation. Local rules produce a wellness score and review flags. When configured, the Manus API uses a predefined prompt to provide general wellness guidance and follow-up conversation. Medical officers can review overall crew status and each astronaut’s composite health trend over the last 14 days.

Our intended impact is to help astronauts understand changes in their well-being and support informed medical review throughout a long mission. Combining readings with self-reported experiences creates a broader picture than either source alone. Our creative approach makes the person—not a spreadsheet—the starting point: an interactive body for exploration, a guide for understanding, and crew-level trends for supervision.

We used React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the interface; Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for the interactive body; and Recharts for visualizations. Python and NumPy support readiness-model inference, while server-side TypeScript endpoints connect the optional Manus API guidance service. Browser state and local storage connect the demo workflows. No physical wearable hardware is integrated yet; current telemetry is simulated.

NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework informed our physical and psychological health focus. We considered usability, individual baseline differences, sensitive health information, and the limitations of applying terrestrial training data to spaceflight. Current authentication and privacy controls are demo-level. Real wearable integration, stronger authorization and data minimization, mission-connectivity testing, and spaceflight validation are next steps. AstroVitals supports awareness and medical review—not diagnosis or replacement of the flight surgeon.
